title: Σαρπηδόνος πτῶσις
about: Sarpedon throws again and misses; Patroclus’ spear strikes him in the chest and he falls like an oak or a tall pine, or a bull killed by a lion. Dying, he calls on Glaucus to rally the Lycians, then to fight for his body himself, lest he be a shame to him for ever; Patroclus sets his heel on him and draws out the spear, and the midriff with it, while the Myrmidons hold the dead man’s horses. Glaucus, wounded in the arm by Teucer and unable to fight, prays to Apollo, who stops the pain and the bleeding and gives him might. He rouses the Lycians, then goes to Polydamas, Agenor, Aeneas and Hector and shames Hector for forgetting the allies who die for him. Grief seizes the Trojans, since Sarpedon was the prop of their city, and Hector leads them on, while Patroclus rouses the Achaeans and the two Ajaxes, wishing the outrage that Glaucus fears. The two sides close over the body, and Zeus lays a baneful night over the battle.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ αὖ Σαρπηδὼν μὲν ἀπήμβροτε δουρὶ φαεινῷ,
Πατρόκλου δ’ ὑπὲρ ὦμον ἀριστερὸν ἤλυθ’ ἀκωκὴ
ἔγχεος, οὐδ’ ἔβαλ’ αὐτόν·
sentences.i: Then Sarpedon, in his turn, missed with his shining spear, and the tip of the spear went over Patroclus’ left shoulder and did not hit him;
sentences.n: This part opens in the middle of the duel on which the last one ended: ἔνθ’ αὖ ‘then, in turn’ is Sarpedon’s second throw (his first, at 16.466–468, had missed Patroclus and hit the horse Pedasus). ἀπήμβροτε ‘missed’ is an aorist, with δουρί, the dative of the spear, ‘with the spear’, and φαεινῷ ‘shining’ its stock epithet. ἤλυθ’ is the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι (= ἦλθε); its subject is ἀκωκή ‘tip’, with ἔγχεος ‘of the spear’ held over to the next line, and ὑπὲρ ὦμον ἀριστερόν is ‘over the left shoulder’. Lines 478–479, as far as αὐτόν, are also 5.16–17, there of Diomedes’ shoulder. The subject of οὐδ’ ἔβαλ’ ‘nor did he hit’ is not restated: it is Sarpedon or his spear, with the same sense.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὕστερος ὄρνυτο χαλκῷ
Πάτροκλος·
sentences.l:
and he, later, rushed on with the bronze,
Patroclus;
sentences.i: and then Patroclus rushed on with the bronze;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is the article as a pronoun, and the name it stands for is held back to the start of the next line, which puts Patroclus’ answer in suspense. ὕστερος ‘later’ means he threw after Sarpedon. ὄρνυτο is a past tense of the middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, which in the middle is ‘rush on’, and χαλκῷ ‘with the bronze’ is the spear. The half-line ὃ δ’ ὕστερος ὄρνυτο χαλκῷ is also the end of 5.17.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ οὐχ ἅλιον βέλος ἔκφυγε χειρός,
ἀλλ’ ἔβαλ’ ἔνθ’ ἄρα τε φρένες ἔρχαται ἀμφ’ ἁδινὸν κῆρ.
sentences.l:
and from his hand the shaft did not escape in vain,
but hit where indeed the midriffs are shut about the thronging heart.
sentences.i: and his shaft did not leave his hand in vain, but hit where the midriff is shut about the thronging heart.
sentences.n: ἅλιον here is ἅλιος ‘in vain’, not the ἅλιος ‘of the sea’; with βέλος ‘shaft’ it is the phrase of 4.498, and the whole first line is also 5.18, whose English it keeps. τοῦ is ‘his’, separated from χειρός. ἔρχαται is the third plural perfect passive of εἴργω ‘shut in’, with the Ionic ending -αται, and its subject is φρένες. Here φρένες is the bodily part and not the mind (where it is ‘wits’): ‘midriff’ is our word, and which organs about the heart Homer means is not known. ἁδινόν ‘thronging’ is the word used of bees at 2.87 and of a heart at Odyssey 19.516, and what it says of a heart is not known. The subject of ἔβαλ’ is the shaft or Patroclus, with the same sense.

sentences.t:
ἤριπε δ’ ὡς ὅτε τις δρῦς ἤριπεν ἢ ἀχερωῒς
ἠὲ πίτυς βλωθρή, τήν τ’ οὔρεσι τέκτονες ἄνδρες
ἐξέταμον πελέκεσσι νεήκεσι νήϊον εἶναι·
sentences.i: He fell as an oak falls, or a white poplar, or a tall pine, that builders cut down on the mountains with newly sharpened axes to be ship’s timber;
sentences.n: ἤριπε is an aorist of ἐρείπω ‘fall in ruin’; it is said of Sarpedon and then, with ὡς ὅτε ‘as when’, of the tree, so the one fall sits inside the other, and the English puts the simile in the present, as a general truth. The three trees are δρῦς ‘oak’, ἀχερωΐς ‘white poplar’ (the traditional identification) and πίτυς ‘pine’ with its epithet βλωθρή ‘tall’, a traditional gloss whose origin is not known. τήν τ’ is the relative ‘which’ with epic τε, and ἐξέταμον is the aorist ‘cut down’ (the augment sits between ἐκ- and the stem). πελέκεσσι νεήκεσι ‘with newly sharpened axes’ is the instrument, and νήϊον εἶναι ‘to be ship-timber’ is the adjective νήϊος ‘of a ship’ with an infinitive of purpose. The three lines are the same as 13.389–391, where Asius falls, and have the same English.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὃ πρόσθ’ ἵππων καὶ δίφρου κεῖτο τανυσθεὶς
βεβρυχὼς κόνιος δεδραγμένος αἱματοέσσης.
sentences.l:
so he in front of the horses and the chariot lay stretched out,
roaring, clutching at the bloody dust.
sentences.i: So he lay stretched out in front of his horses and chariot, roaring, clutching at the bloody dust.
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ answers the simile. πρόσθ’ takes the genitives ἵππων and δίφρου ‘in front of the horses and the chariot’; κεῖτο is the imperfect of κεῖμαι ‘lie’ and τανυσθείς the aorist passive participle of τανύω ‘stretch’, ‘laid out at full length’. βεβρυχώς is a perfect participle, and ‘roaring’ is the usual sense; whether it is roaring or gnashing the teeth is not certain. δεδραγμένος, the perfect participle of δράσσομαι ‘grasp’, takes the genitive κόνιος ‘of the dust’, so ‘clutching at’, and αἱματοέσσης ‘bloody’ agrees with it. The lines are those of 13.392–393.

sentences.t:
ἠΰτε ταῦρον ἔπεφνε λέων ἀγέληφι μετελθὼν
αἴθωνα μεγάθυμον ἐν εἰλιπόδεσσι βόεσσι,
ὤλετό τε στενάχων ὑπὸ γαμφηλῇσι λέοντος,
sentences.l:
As a lion kills a bull, having come among the herd,
a fire-bright, great-hearted one, among the rolling-gaited cattle,
and he perishes, groaning, under the jaws of the lion,
sentences.i: As a lion kills a fire-bright, great-hearted bull, having come among the herd of cattle of rolling gait, and the bull perishes, groaning, under the lion’s jaws,
sentences.n: ἠΰτε ‘as, like’ begins a second simile. ἔπεφνε ‘kills’ and ὤλετο ‘perishes’ are aorists of a simile, which say what happens in general, so the English has the present, as for ἔκλυε ‘hears’ at 4.455. ἀγέληφι is ἀγέλη ‘herd’ with the old suffix -φι, ‘among the herd’, with μετελθών ‘having come among’. αἴθωνα is the epithet ‘fire-bright’ (the colour is not decided), μεγάθυμον ‘great-hearted’, and ἐν εἰλιπόδεσσι βόεσσι ‘among the rolling-gaited cattle’ is the Odyssey’s formula. γαμφηλῇσι is the epic dative plural of γαμφηλαί ‘jaws’. The next unit, with ὣς, gives the thing compared.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὑπὸ Πατρόκλῳ Λυκίων ἀγὸς ἀσπιστάων
κτεινόμενος μενέαινε, φίλον δ’ ὀνόμηνεν ἑταῖρον·
sentences.l:
so under Patroclus the leader of the Lycians, the shield-bearers,
being killed, was eager, and his dear companion he named;
sentences.i: so, at the hands of Patroclus, the leader of the Lycian shield-bearers, as he was being killed, was full of eagerness, and called his dear companion by name;
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ gives the thing compared. ὑπὸ Πατρόκλῳ is ‘under Patroclus’, that is, at his hands. Λυκίων ἀγὸς ἀσπιστάων ‘leader of the Lycians, the shield-bearers’ has two genitive plurals, the second a noun ἀσπιστής ‘shield-bearer’ in apposition. κτεινόμενος ‘being killed’ is a present passive participle, and μενέαινε is an imperfect of μενεαίνω ‘be eager’; the verb has no object, and the Greek does not say what he was eager for; the call to Glaucus that follows shows where his mind is. φίλον … ἑταῖρον ‘dear companion’ is the object of ὀνόμηνεν, ‘named, called by name’, and the companion is Glaucus, whom the speech addresses.

sentences.t:
Γλαῦκε πέπον πολεμιστὰ μετ’ ἀνδράσι νῦν σε μάλα χρὴ
αἰχμητήν τ’ ἔμεναι καὶ θαρσαλέον πολεμιστήν·
sentences.l:
“Glaucus, good one, warrior, among men now it very much behoves you
to be a spearman and a bold warrior;
sentences.i: “Glaucus, my good fellow, warrior among men, now you very much must be a spearman and a bold warrior;
sentences.n: Γλαῦκε is the vocative of Γλαῦκος, Sarpedon’s fellow-commander. πέπον is an address whose meaning is not known (‘good fellow’ is the traditional reading), and πολεμιστά is the vocative of πολεμιστής ‘warrior’, which comes again, in the accusative, at the end of the next line, so the word stands twice. μετ’ ἀνδράσι ‘among men’ may go with πολεμιστά or with the whole sentence. νῦν σε μάλα χρή is ‘now you very much must’: χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes σε with an infinitive, and ἔμεναι is the Homeric infinitive of εἰμί, with αἰχμητήν ‘spearman’ and θαρσαλέον ‘bold’ as its predicates. Sarpedon’s speech begins here and runs to 501; line 493 is also 5.602.

sentences.t: νῦν τοι ἐελδέσθω πόλεμος κακός, εἰ θοός ἐσσι.
sentences.l: Now let evil war be wished for by you, if swift you are.
sentences.i: Now let evil war be your longing, if you are swift.
sentences.n: ἐελδέσθω is the third singular imperative of ἐέλδομαι ‘long for’, with πόλεμος ‘war’ as its subject and τοι (= σοι) ‘to you’ as the person: ‘let war be what you long for’. The construction is unusual: elsewhere the one who longs is the subject of ἐέλδομαι (13.638, 14.276), so πόλεμος as subject is odd, and the sense given here is the traditional one. κακός ‘evil’ is said of the war; εἰ θοός ἐσσι ‘if you are swift’ makes speed the proof of a fighter, and ἐσσι is the Homeric second singular of εἰμί.

sentences.t:
πρῶτα μὲν ὄτρυνον Λυκίων ἡγήτορας ἄνδρας
πάντῃ ἐποιχόμενος Σαρπηδόνος ἀμφιμάχεσθαι·
sentences.l:
First, on the one hand, urge on the leader-men of the Lycians,
everywhere going to and fro, around Sarpedon to fight;
sentences.i: First urge on the leaders of the Lycians, going all about to fight around Sarpedon;
sentences.n: πρῶτα μέν ‘first, to begin with’ is answered by αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα ‘but then’ in the next line. ὄτρυνον is the aorist imperative of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’ (the present imperative is ὄτρυνε, 501). Λυκίων ἡγήτορας ἄνδρας is ‘the leaders of the Lycians, men’, with ἄνδρας in apposition, ‘leading men’. ἐποιχόμενος ‘going to and fro’ (ἐποίχομαι, as at 5.720) agrees with the ‘you’ of the imperative, and ἀμφιμάχεσθαι takes the genitive Σαρπηδόνος, ‘fight around Sarpedon’; he calls himself by name. The line 496 comes again at 533, where Glaucus does as he was told.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα καὶ αὐτὸς ἐμεῦ πέρι μάρναο χαλκῷ.
sentences.l: but then, you yourself also, around me fight with the bronze.
sentences.i: and after that fight for me yourself too, with the bronze.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα ‘but then’ answers πρῶτα μέν of 495. μάρναο is the second singular present imperative of μάρναμαι ‘fight’, with the middle ending -ο (from -σο, the σ lost), and καὶ αὐτός is ‘you yourself too’. ἐμεῦ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ (= ἐμοῦ), and πέρι with the genitive is ‘around, over’: fight round me, for my sake. χαλκῷ ‘with the bronze’ is the weapon.

sentences.t:
σοὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ καὶ ἔπειτα κατηφείη καὶ ὄνειδος
ἔσσομαι ἤματα πάντα διαμπερές, εἴ κέ μ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
τεύχεα συλήσωσι νεῶν ἐν ἀγῶνι πεσόντα.
sentences.l:
For to you I even afterwards a shame and a reproach
shall be, all days, without ceasing, if me the Achaeans
armour should strip, fallen in the gathering of the ships.
sentences.i: For I shall be a shame and a reproach to you hereafter too, for all days, without ceasing, if the Achaeans strip me of my armour as I lie fallen in the gathering-place of the ships.
sentences.n: σοί ‘to you’ is the person who would bear the shame, and ἔσσομαι is the epic future of εἰμί (‘I shall be’, with the doubled σ). κατηφείη ‘shame’ is from the adjective κατηφής ‘downcast’, a downcast look, traditionally that of a man with his eyes lowered, and its exact sense, shame felt or shame caused, is hard to fix; ὄνειδος is ‘reproach’. ἤματα πάντα ‘all days’ is an accusative of time, and διαμπερές ‘without ceasing’. εἴ κε with the aorist subjunctive συλήσωσι is ‘if they should strip’, with μ’ and τεύχεα ‘armour’ as a double accusative, ‘strip me of armour’, and πεσόντα ‘fallen’ agrees with μ’. καὶ ἔπειτα is ‘even afterwards, hereafter’. ἀγών is the place where men gather, here ‘the gathering of the ships’ (ἐν ἀγῶνι also at 16.239). The last line is also 15.428.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔχεο κρατερῶς, ὄτρυνε δὲ λαὸν ἅπαντα.
sentences.l: But hold yourself strongly, and urge on the people, all of it.”
sentences.i: But hold on strongly, and urge on the whole army.”
sentences.n: ἔχεο is the second singular imperative middle of ἔχω ‘hold’, ‘hold yourself, hold on’, and κρατερῶς is ‘strongly’. ὄτρυνε is the present imperative of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, with λαὸν ἅπαντα ‘all the people’, the whole Lycian army, as object. With this last order Sarpedon’s speech ends.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα μιν εἰπόντα τέλος θανάτοιο κάλυψεν
ὀφθαλμοὺς ῥῖνάς θ’·
sentences.l:
So then him, having spoken, the end of death covered,
eyes and nostrils;
sentences.i: When he had spoken so, the end that death brings covered his eyes and nostrils;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα ‘so, then’ closes the speech, and μιν and εἰπόντα go together, ‘him, having spoken’. τέλος θανάτοιο ‘the end of death’ is the formula of 5.553, death as a limit that comes down and covers. ὀφθαλμοὺς ῥῖνάς θ’ are accusatives of the part affected, ‘covered him in respect of eyes and nostrils’, with ῥῖνας the plural of ῥίς ‘nose’, so ‘nostrils’, and θ’ = τε ‘and’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ λὰξ ἐν στήθεσι βαίνων
ἐκ χροὸς ἕλκε δόρυ, προτὶ δὲ φρένες αὐτῷ ἕποντο·
sentences.l:
and he, with his heel on his chest, stepping,
from the flesh drew the spear, and with it the midriffs followed;
sentences.i: Setting his heel on his chest, he drew the spear out of the flesh, and the midriff followed it;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Patroclus, whom the verse does not name, and the subject changes from the dying man. λὰξ ἐν στήθεσι βαίνων is the phrase of 13.618, ‘with his heel on his chest’, the plural στήθεσι being ‘chest’. ἕλκε is an imperfect without augment, ‘was drawing’, and ἐκ χροός is ‘out of the flesh’. φρένες is again the bodily part, ‘midriff’ (as at 481; as the mind it is ‘wits’), and which organs are meant is not known. προτί is the epic form of πρός, and with ἕποντο ‘followed’ and αὐτῷ ‘with it’ (the spear) it says the midriff came away along with the spear. Homer states this plainly and does not soften it.

sentences.t: τοῖο δ’ ἅμα ψυχήν τε καὶ ἔγχεος ἐξέρυσ’ αἰχμήν.
sentences.l: and at the same time of him the soul and of the spear the point he drew out.
sentences.i: and at the same moment drew out both his soul and the point of the spear.
sentences.n: τοῖο is the epic genitive of τό (= τοῦ), ‘his’, the dying man’s, with ψυχήν ‘soul’; ἅμα … τε καὶ is ‘at the same time … both … and’. ψυχή is the life that leaves the body, ‘soul’, as in 5.696. ἔγχεος αἰχμήν is ‘the point of the spear’, αἰχμή being ‘point’ where ἀκωκή at 478 is ‘tip’. ἐξέρυσ’ is the aorist of ἐξερύω ‘draw out’, with its ending elided.

sentences.t:
Μυρμιδόνες δ’ αὐτοῦ σχέθον ἵππους φυσιόωντας
ἱεμένους φοβέεσθαι, ἐπεὶ λίπον ἅρματ’ ἀνάκτων.
sentences.l:
And the Myrmidons held there the horses, snorting,
eager to flee, since they had left the chariots of their lords.
sentences.i: The Myrmidons held back the snorting horses there, eager to flee, since they had left the chariots of their lords.
sentences.n: Μυρμιδόνες ‘Myrmidons’ are Achilles’ men, who follow Patroclus. αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘there, on the spot’; σχέθον is an unaugmented aorist (= ἔσχον ‘held back’). φυσιόωντας ‘snorting’ is the stock word for horses’ breath, and it and ἱεμένους ‘eager’ agree with ἵππους. φοβέεσθαι is a present infinitive of φοβέομαι ‘flee in fear’, and ἅρματ’ ἀνάκτων ‘the chariots of their lords’ is the phrase of 16.371; the subject of λίπον ‘they had left’ is the horses, whose lords have fallen.

sentences.t: Γλαύκῳ δ’ αἰνὸν ἄχος γένετο φθογγῆς ἀΐοντι·
sentences.l: And to Glaucus fearsome grief came, as he heard the voice;
sentences.i: And fearsome grief came over Glaucus as he heard that voice;
sentences.n: Γλαύκῳ is the dative ‘to Glaucus’, the Lycian leader who was named at the start of Sarpedon’s speech; the paragraph turns from Patroclus to him. αἰνὸν ἄχος ‘fearsome grief’ is the phrase of 4.169, and γένετο is an aorist without augment, ‘came to be’. ἀΐοντι ‘as he heard’ is a participle in the dative, agreeing with Γλαύκῳ, and what is heard, φθογγῆς ‘the voice’, is in the genitive, as sounds are with verbs of hearing; the voice is Sarpedon’s.

sentences.t: ὠρίνθη δέ οἱ ἦτορ ὅ τ’ οὐ δύνατο προσαμῦναι.
sentences.l: and his heart was stirred up, because he was not able to come to the defence.
sentences.i: and his heart was stirred because he could not come to his defence.
sentences.n: ὠρίνθη is the aorist passive of ὀρίνω ‘stir up’, and its subject is ἦτορ ‘heart’, with οἱ (= αὐτῷ) ‘in him’. ὅ τ’ is the neuter relative used as ‘because’ (the same as ὅτι). δύνατο is an imperfect of δύναμαι ‘be able’, and προσαμῦναι the aorist infinitive of προσαμύνω ‘come to the defence’, with no object given (Sarpedon is meant).

sentences.t: χειρὶ δ’ ἑλὼν ἐπίεζε βραχίονα·
sentences.l: With his hand taking hold, he pressed his arm;
sentences.i: He took hold of his arm with his hand and pressed it;
sentences.n: ἑλών is the aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘take’, ‘having taken hold’, with χειρί ‘with his hand’, and ἐπίεζε is the imperfect of πιέζω ‘press, squeeze’. βραχίονα is the upper arm; the Greek does not say whose, and the wound named next shows that it is Glaucus’ own.

sentences.t:
τεῖρε γὰρ αὐτὸν
ἕλκος, ὃ δή μιν Τεῦκρος ἐπεσσύμενον βάλεν ἰῷ
τείχεος ὑψηλοῖο, ἀρὴν ἑτάροισιν ἀμύνων.
sentences.l:
for wore him down
the wound, which indeed him, rushing on, Teucer struck with an arrow
at the high wall, ruin for his companions warding off.
sentences.i: for the wound was wearing him down, the one Teucer, warding off ruin for his companions, had given him with an arrow as he rushed at the high wall.
sentences.n: τεῖρε is an imperfect of τείρω ‘wear down’, with ἕλκος ‘wound’ as subject, and ὃ δή is ‘which, as we know’: the wound was given at 12.387–391, when Teucer shot Glaucus as he went at the wall. ἐπεσσύμενον ‘rushing on’ (agreeing with μιν, Glaucus) goes with τείχεος ὑψηλοῖο ‘the high wall’, the same words as 12.388; the genitive is taken as the goal, ‘at the wall’. βάλεν is an unaugmented aorist, ‘struck’, ἰῷ the dative of ἰός ‘arrow’, and μιν ‘him’. ἀρὴν ἑτάροισιν ἀμύνων is ‘warding ruin off for his companions’ (as at 12.334), with ἀμύνων the participle of Teucer.

sentences.t: εὐχόμενος δ’ ἄρα εἶπεν ἑκηβόλῳ Ἀπόλλωνι·
sentences.l: And praying, then, he spoke to far-shooting Apollo:
sentences.i: Then, praying, he said to far-shooting Apollo:
sentences.n: εὐχόμενος ‘praying’ is a participle of εὔχομαι, a verb that also means ‘boast’. ἑκηβόλῳ ‘far-shooting’ is the stock epithet of Apollo, translated each time; the usual explanation is ἑκάς ‘far’ and βάλλω ‘shoot’, and it is not certain. The dative ἑκηβόλῳ Ἀπόλλωνι follows εἶπεν. The prayer that follows is Glaucus’ speech to the god.

sentences.t:
κλῦθι ἄναξ ὅς που Λυκίης ἐν πίονι δήμῳ
εἲς ἢ ἐνὶ Τροίῃ·
sentences.l:
“Hear, lord, you who somewhere in Lycia’s rich land
are, or in Troy;
sentences.i: “Hear, lord, you who are somewhere in the rich land of Lycia, or in Troy;
sentences.n: κλῦθι is the aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, the stock opening of a prayer, and ἄναξ is ‘lord’. ὅς is a relative with που ‘somewhere, perhaps’, and its verb is εἲς, which is the second singular ‘you are’ of εἰμί (the grave accent is as the text prints it), so the clause is ‘you who are somewhere …’, said of the god. Λυκίης ἐν πίονι δήμῳ ‘in Lycia’s rich land’ is the phrase of 16.437, Lycia being both the god’s land and Glaucus’ own; the prayer covers Troy too, in case the god is there.

sentences.t:
δύνασαι δὲ σὺ πάντοσ’ ἀκούειν
ἀνέρι κηδομένῳ, ὡς νῦν ἐμὲ κῆδος ἱκάνει.
sentences.l:
but you are able, you, everywhere to hear
a man grieved, as now upon me trouble comes.
sentences.i: but you are able to hear a man in distress everywhere, as trouble now comes upon me.
sentences.n: δύνασαι ‘you are able’ is a second singular, with σύ added for strength, and πάντοσ’ is πάντοσε ‘in every direction, everywhere’. ἀνέρι is the epic form of the dative ἀνδρί ‘a man’, the one who is heard, with ἀκούειν ‘to hear’, and κηδομένῳ ‘grieved’ is the participle of κήδομαι ‘be distressed’ in the same case. κῆδος ‘trouble’ is the noun from the same root, and ἱκάνει ‘comes upon, reaches’, with ἐμέ ‘me’ its object and ὡς ‘as, in the way that’.

sentences.t:
ἕλκος μὲν γὰρ ἔχω τόδε καρτερόν, ἀμφὶ δέ μοι χεὶρ
ὀξείῃς ὀδύνῃσιν ἐλήλαται, οὐδέ μοι αἷμα
τερσῆναι δύναται, βαρύθει δέ μοι ὦμος ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ·
sentences.i: I have this severe wound, and my hand is beset on every side with sharp pains, and my blood cannot dry, and my shoulder is weighed down by it;
sentences.n: ἕλκος … τόδε καρτερόν ‘this strong wound’ is a phrase that comes again at 523. ἐλήλαται is a perfect passive of ἐλαύνω, literally ‘has been driven’, with ἀμφί ‘about’ and ὀξείῃς ὀδύνῃσιν ‘with sharp pains’; the picture of pains driven round the hand is not clear, and ‘beset on every side’ gives the sense. μοι is the dative ‘my’ (three times, at 517–519). τερσῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of τέρσομαι ‘become dry’, so the wound is still bleeding. βαρύθει is ‘is weighed down, is heavy’, ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ ‘under it’ (the wound).

sentences.t:
ἔγχος δ’ οὐ δύναμαι σχεῖν ἔμπεδον, οὐδὲ μάχεσθαι
ἐλθὼν δυσμενέεσσιν.
sentences.l:
and the spear I am not able to hold steady, nor to fight,
going, against enemies.
sentences.i: I cannot hold my spear steady, nor go and fight the enemy.
sentences.n: σχεῖν is the aorist infinitive of ἔχω ‘hold’, with ἔμπεδον ‘steadily’ as an adverb (‘firm, steady’, as at 5.527), and δύναμαι is ‘I am able’. ἐλθών ‘having gone’ with μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ is ‘go and fight’. δυσμενέεσσιν is the dative plural of δυσμενής ‘hostile’, here ‘enemies’, with the epic ending -εσσι.

sentences.t:
ἀνὴρ δ’ ὤριστος ὄλωλε
Σαρπηδὼν Διὸς υἱός·
sentences.l:
and a man, the best, has perished,
Sarpedon, son of Zeus;
sentences.i: and the best of men has perished, Sarpedon, son of Zeus;
sentences.n: ὤριστος is ὁ ἄριστος, with the article fused to the adjective, so ἀνὴρ ὤριστος is ‘the best man’; ὄλωλε is the perfect of ὄλλυμι, ‘has perished, is lost’. Σαρπηδών is in apposition, and Διὸς υἱός ‘son of Zeus’ sets up the charge in the next unit.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ οὐ οὗ παιδὸς ἀμύνει.
sentences.l: but he not of his own child wards off.
sentences.i: but he does not ward off harm from his own son.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘but he’ is Zeus, who is not named; the pronoun answers Διός in the unit before. οὐ οὗ is the negative οὐ and οὗ ‘his own’, the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν (not the relative). ἀμύνει is ‘wards off’, and with the genitive παιδός it is ‘ward off from his child’, that is, protect him; elsewhere (at 512) the verb takes a dative of the people helped.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ πέρ μοι ἄναξ τόδε καρτερὸν ἕλκος ἄκεσσαι,
κοίμησον δ’ ὀδύνας, δὸς δὲ κράτος, ὄφρ’ ἑτάροισι
κεκλόμενος Λυκίοισιν ἐποτρύνω πολεμίζειν,
αὐτός τ’ ἀμφὶ νέκυι κατατεθνηῶτι μάχωμαι.
sentences.l:
But you at least, lord, this strong wound for me heal,
put to sleep the pains, and give strength, so that to my companions
calling, to the Lycians, I may urge them on to fight,
and myself around the dead man, him who has died, may fight.”
sentences.i: But you at least, lord, heal this severe wound for me, put my pains to sleep, and give me strength, so that I may call to my companions the Lycians and urge them on to fight, and may fight myself around the dead man.”
sentences.n: σύ πέρ ‘you at least’ narrows the plea to the one god who can help, and ἄκεσσαι is the aorist imperative middle of ἀκέομαι ‘heal’. κοίμησον ‘put to sleep’ and δός ‘give’ are aorist imperatives, and κράτος is ‘strength’ (1.509). ὄφρα with the subjunctives ἐποτρύνω ‘I may urge on’ and μάχωμαι ‘I may fight’ gives the purpose; κεκλόμενος is the participle of κέκλομαι ‘call to’, with the datives ἑτάροισι Λυκίοισιν ‘to my companions the Lycians’. νέκυι is ‘the dead man’ (Sarpedon’s body), and κατατεθνηῶτι, a perfect participle of καταθνῄσκω, adds ‘him who has died’; the same words stand at 565. Glaucus asks for strength to fight on, not for rescue; the prayer ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος, τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων.
sentences.l: So he spoke, praying, and him heard Phoebus Apollo.
sentences.i: So he prayed, and Phoebus Apollo heard him.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος ‘so he spoke, praying’ is the usual close of a prayer, and Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων is ‘Phoebus Apollo’. ἔκλυε is an aorist of κλύω ‘hear’, and with τοῦ it takes the genitive of the person heard. The prayer is answered at once. The whole line stands at 1.43, where Chryses prays to the same god, and at 1.457.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα παῦσ’ ὀδύνας ἀπὸ δ’ ἕλκεος ἀργαλέοιο
αἷμα μέλαν τέρσηνε, μένος δέ οἱ ἔμβαλε θυμῷ.
sentences.l:
At once he stopped the pains, and from the wound, grievous,
the blood, black, he dried off, and might in his heart he put.
sentences.i: At once he stopped the pains, and dried the black blood from the grievous wound, and put might in his heart.
sentences.n: παῦσ’ is the aorist of παύω ‘stop’, with ὀδύνας ‘pains’ as object. ἀπὸ … τέρσηνε is split (tmesis): ἀποτέρσηνε ‘dried off’, an aorist of τερσαίνω ‘make dry’ (beside τέρσομαι ‘become dry’ at 519), with αἷμα μέλαν ‘black blood’ for object, and ἕλκεος ἀργαλέοιο ‘grievous wound’ in the genitive, with the epic ending -εος. μένος ‘might’ and θυμῷ ‘heart’ answer the request for κράτος at 524; ἔμβαλε is ‘put in’, and οἱ ‘in him’ is a dative.

sentences.t:
Γλαῦκος δ’ ἔγνω ᾗσιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶ γήθησέν τε
ὅττί οἱ ὦκ’ ἤκουσε μέγας θεὸς εὐξαμένοιο.
sentences.l:
And Glaucus knew in his own wits and rejoiced
that for him quickly heard the great god, as he prayed.
sentences.i: Glaucus knew it in his own mind and rejoiced that the great god had quickly heard him as he prayed.
sentences.n: ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘recognize, perceive’, and ᾗσιν is the possessive ‘his own’, agreeing with φρεσί ‘in his own mind’, not a relative. γήθησέν τε ‘and rejoiced’ has its ν of movement. ὅττι is ὅτι ‘that’ with the epic doubled τ, and ὦκ’ is ὠκά ‘quickly’. ἤκουσε takes the genitive εὐξαμένοιο, an aorist middle participle, ‘as he prayed’, and οἱ ‘for him’ is a dative of interest. μέγας θεός ‘the great god’ is Apollo, who is not named.

sentences.t:
πρῶτα μὲν ὄτρυνεν Λυκίων ἡγήτορας ἄνδρας
πάντῃ ἐποιχόμενος Σαρπηδόνος ἀμφιμάχεσθαι·
sentences.l:
First, on the one hand, he urged on the leader-men of the Lycians,
everywhere going to and fro, around Sarpedon to fight;
sentences.i: First he urged on the leaders of the Lycians, going all about to fight around Sarpedon;
sentences.n: These two lines carry out Sarpedon’s orders of 495–496, word for word except that ὄτρυνεν ‘he urged on’ is a past tense where ὄτρυνον was the imperative, and so they have the same English; the repetition is the point, since the order is obeyed as given. πρῶτα μέν ‘first’ is answered by αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα ‘but then’ in the next unit, and the subject is Glaucus. ἐποιχόμενος ‘going to and fro’ is the participle of ἐποίχομαι, and ἀμφιμάχεσθαι takes the genitive Σαρπηδόνος ‘around Sarpedon’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα μετὰ Τρῶας κίε μακρὰ βιβάσθων
Πουλυδάμαντ’ ἔπι Πανθοΐδην καὶ Ἀγήνορα δῖον,
βῆ δὲ μετ’ Αἰνείαν τε καὶ Ἕκτορα χαλκοκορυστήν,
sentences.l:
but then among the Trojans he went, taking long strides,
to Polydamas, Panthous’-son, and heavenly Agenor,
and went after Aeneas and Hector, bronze-armed,
sentences.i: and then he went among the Trojans, taking long strides, to Polydamas, son of Panthous, and heavenly Agenor, and went after Aeneas and Hector, armed in bronze,
sentences.n: κίε is a past tense of κίω ‘go’, without augment. μακρὰ βιβάσθων ‘taking long strides’ has an old participle of βιβάω, the same words as at 13.809 and 15.676 and the same sense as μακρὰ βιβάς at 15.307. Πουλυδάμαντ’ ἔπι is ‘to Polydamas’, with ἔπι placed after its accusative, and Πανθοΐδην is the patronymic ‘son of Panthous’. Ἀγήνορα δῖον is ‘heavenly Agenor’, δῖος being the stock epithet. βῆ δὲ μετ’ Αἰνείαν is ‘and went after Aeneas’, μετά with the accusative being ‘in quest of’, and χαλκοκορυστήν ‘armed in bronze’ is the epithet of Hector. The sentence runs on to the speech introduction in the next line.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱστάμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: and standing close by, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and, standing close beside him, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: This is the stock introduction of a speech: ἀγχοῦ ‘close by’, ἱστάμενος ‘standing’, ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’, translated the same way every time, and προσηύδα ‘he spoke to’. The person addressed is Hector, whom the speech names, and it runs to 547.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ νῦν δὴ πάγχυ λελασμένος εἰς ἐπικούρων,
οἳ σέθεν εἵνεκα τῆλε φίλων καὶ πατρίδος αἴης
θυμὸν ἀποφθινύθουσι·
sentences.i: “Hector, you have now quite forgotten the allies, who for your sake, far from their friends and their native land, are wasting their lives away;
sentences.n: νῦν δὴ πάγχυ is ‘now indeed wholly’ (πάγχυ ‘altogether’, as at 13.747). λελασμένος is a perfect middle participle of λανθάνομαι ‘forget’ and takes the genitive ἐπικούρων ‘the allies’ (ἐπίκουρος ‘ally’). εἰς here is not the preposition ‘into’ but the second singular ‘you are’ of εἰμί, the form printed at 515 with an accent (here it has none), and with the participle it makes ‘you have forgotten’. σέθεν is the epic genitive of σύ (= σοῦ), and εἵνεκα ‘for the sake of’ follows it. τῆλε ‘far’ takes the genitives φίλων ‘friends’ and πατρίδος αἴης ‘native land’. ἀποφθινύθουσι is a present, ‘are wasting away’, and takes θυμόν as object, the life-spirit that leaves a dying man; at 5.643 the verb has no object and is ‘dying off’. Glaucus begins by rebuking Hector.

sentences.t: σὺ δ’ οὐκ ἐθέλεις ἐπαμύνειν.
sentences.l: and you are not willing to come to the defence.
sentences.i: yet you are unwilling to come to their defence.
sentences.n: σὺ δ’ ‘but you’ has σύ for emphasis. οὐκ ἐθέλεις is ‘you are unwilling’, and ἐπαμύνειν is the infinitive of ἐπαμύνω ‘come to the defence’, with no object given; the allies are understood (‘their’ in the English).

sentences.t:
κεῖται Σαρπηδὼν Λυκίων ἀγὸς ἀσπιστάων,
ὃς Λυκίην εἴρυτο δίκῃσί τε καὶ σθένεϊ ᾧ·
sentences.l:
Lies Sarpedon, leader of the Lycians, the shield-bearers,
who Lycia guarded with justice and with his own strength;
sentences.i: Sarpedon lies there, the leader of the Lycian shield-bearers, who guarded Lycia by his justice and his own strength;
sentences.n: κεῖται ‘lies’ is said of the dead man, Λυκίων ἀγὸς ἀσπιστάων is ‘leader of the Lycians, the shield-bearers’, as at 490. εἴρυτο is a past tense of the middle of ἐρύομαι (= ῥύομαι) ‘protect, guard’, a different verb from ἐρύω ‘draw’; Λυκίην is its object. δίκῃσι is the epic dative plural of δίκη ‘justice’, so ‘by his justice’, and σθένεϊ ᾧ is ‘with his own strength’, ᾧ being the possessive ὅς ‘his own’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ὑπὸ Πατρόκλῳ δάμασ’ ἔγχεϊ χάλκεος Ἄρης.
sentences.l: him under Patroclus with the spear subdued bronze Ares.
sentences.i: Ares in bronze has overcome him, at the hands of Patroclus, with the spear.
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ‘and him’ comes first, for emphasis. ὑπὸ Πατρόκλῳ is ‘under Patroclus’, as at 490, and ἔγχεϊ is the dative ‘with the spear’. δάμασ’ is the aorist of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, which means kill. χάλκεος Ἄρης ‘Ares in bronze’ is the god, and also war itself that kills with bronze.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ φίλοι πάρστητε, νεμεσσήθητε δὲ θυμῷ,
μὴ ἀπὸ τεύχε’ ἕλωνται, ἀεικίσσωσι δὲ νεκρὸν
Μυρμιδόνες, Δαναῶν κεχολωμένοι ὅσσοι ὄλοντο,
τοὺς ἐπὶ νηυσὶ θοῇσιν ἐπέφνομεν ἐγχείῃσιν.
sentences.l:
But, friends, stand by, and feel resentment in your heart,
lest they take off the armour, and treat unseemly the corpse,
the Myrmidons, angered for the Danaans, as many as perished,
whom by the swift ships we killed with spears.”
sentences.i: But, friends, stand by him, and feel resentment in your hearts, lest the Myrmidons strip off his armour and abuse his corpse, angered for all the Danaans who perished, whom we killed with our spears beside the swift ships.”
sentences.n: πάρστητε is παραστῆτε, the aorist imperative of παρίστημι ‘stand by’, with the vowel dropped, and no object is given; the body is meant. νεμεσσήθητε is an aorist (passive in form) imperative of νεμεσσάομαι ‘feel resentment’, here the resentment of men at what is shameful, which is nearer to righteous indignation; English has no one word for it. μὴ … ἕλωνται and ἀεικίσσωσι are aorist subjunctives after μή ‘lest’, and ἀπὸ … ἕλωνται is split (tmesis): ‘take off’ the τεύχε’ ‘armour’. ἀεικίζω ‘treat unseemly’ is from ἀεικής ‘unseemly’ (as at 1.341), and νεκρόν is ‘corpse’. κεχολωμένοι is the perfect participle of χολόω ‘anger’ with the genitive Δαναῶν ‘on account of the Danaans’, and ὅσσοι ὄλοντο is ‘as many as perished’. ἐπέφνομεν is a first plural aorist, ‘we killed’, the ‘we’ being the Trojans and their allies, and ἐγχείῃσιν is the epic dative plural ‘with spears’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατο, Τρῶας δὲ κατὰ κρῆθεν λάβε πένθος
ἄσχετον, οὐκ ἐπιεικτόν, ἐπεί σφισιν ἕρμα πόληος
ἔσκε καὶ ἀλλοδαπός περ ἐών·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and unrestrainable and unyielding grief seized the Trojans from the head down, since he had been the prop of their city, foreigner though he was;
sentences.n: κατὰ κρῆθεν is ‘down from the head’, κρῆθεν being from κάρη ‘head’ with the suffix -θεν ‘from’. λάβε is an aorist without augment, and its subject is πένθος ‘grief’, which ἄσχετον ‘unrestrainable’ and οὐκ ἐπιεικτόν ‘not yielding’ describe, as in Hera’s ‘might’ at 5.892–893. ἕρμα πόληος ‘a prop of the city’ is a figure of speech (a ἕρμα is a support; compare 4.117), with πόληος the epic genitive of πόλις and σφισιν ‘for them’ a dative. ἔσκε is an iterative past of εἰμί (‘was, used to be’), here simply ‘he was’ (the English says ‘had been’ because he is dead), and ἀλλοδαπός περ ἐών ‘foreigner though he was’ has περ ‘even’ with the participle: Sarpedon was a Lycian, not a Trojan.

sentences.t:
πολέες γὰρ ἅμ’ αὐτῷ
λαοὶ ἕποντ’, ἐν δ’ αὐτὸς ἀριστεύεσκε μάχεσθαι·
sentences.l:
for many people along with him
followed, and among them he himself used to be the best at fighting;
sentences.i: for many troops followed along with him, and he himself used to be the best among them at fighting;
sentences.n: πολέες is the epic form of πολλοί ‘many’, and λαοί ‘troops’ is the subject of ἕποντ’ (= ἕποντο ‘were following’), with ἅμ’ αὐτῷ ‘along with him’. ἐν δ’ is ‘and among them’, ἐν as an adverb. ἀριστεύεσκε is the iterative imperfect of ἀριστεύω ‘be the best’, the suffix -εσκε meaning ‘used to’, and μάχεσθαι is an infinitive ‘in fighting’.

sentences.t: βὰν δ’ ἰθὺς Δαναῶν λελιημένοι·
sentences.l: and they went straight at the Danaans, eager;
sentences.i: and eagerly they went straight for the Danaans;
sentences.n: βάν is the aorist of βαίνω without augment (= ἔβησαν, ‘they went’), and ἰθύς ‘straight’ takes the genitive Δαναῶν ‘straight at the Danaans’. λελιημένοι is the perfect participle of λιλαίομαι ‘long, be eager’, here of men on the charge; the subject is the Trojans and their allies.

sentences.t:
ἦρχε δ’ ἄρά σφιν
Ἕκτωρ χωόμενος Σαρπηδόνος.
sentences.l:
and led them
Hector, incensed for Sarpedon.
sentences.i: and Hector led them, incensed over Sarpedon.
sentences.n: ἦρχε is an imperfect of ἄρχω ‘lead’, with the dative σφιν ‘them’ (epic for σφίσιν). χωόμενος ‘incensed’ is the participle of the stock phrase χωόμενος κῆρ, here with the genitive Σαρπηδόνος, ‘on account of Sarpedon’, which gives the cause.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὺς
ὦρσε Μενοιτιάδεω Πατροκλῆος λάσιον κῆρ·
sentences.l:
but the Achaeans
roused of Menoetius’-son Patroclus the shaggy heart;
sentences.i: but the shaggy heart of Patroclus, son of Menoetius, roused the Achaeans;
sentences.n: The subject is λάσιον κῆρ ‘the shaggy heart’ and the object Ἀχαιούς, so in English the order turns round: the heart roused the Achaeans. The phrase names Patroclus by his heart, as 2.851 does Pylaemenes; ‘shaggy’ (λάσιος) is the stock word, and what it says of a heart is not known. ὦρσε is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, Μενοιτιάδεω is the epic genitive of Μενοιτιάδης ‘son of Menoetius’, and Πατροκλῆος is the epic genitive of Πάτροκλος (= Πατρόκλου).

sentences.t: Αἴαντε πρώτω προσέφη μεμαῶτε καὶ αὐτώ·
sentences.l: The two Ajaxes first he addressed, both eager, of themselves too:
sentences.i: He spoke to the two Ajaxes first, both of them eager of their own accord:
sentences.n: Αἴαντε is a dual, ‘the two Ajaxes’, as are πρώτω ‘first’ and the participle μεμαῶτε ‘eager’ (from μέμαα ‘be eager’) that agree with it; αὐτώ is a dual too, ‘themselves’, and καὶ αὐτώ means they were eager of their own accord already. προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’, (the augment sits between πρός and the stem), and its subject is Patroclus, named by his heart in the line before. His speech begins in the next unit and runs to 561.

sentences.t:
Αἴαντε νῦν σφῶϊν ἀμύνεσθαι φίλον ἔστω,
οἷοί περ πάρος ἦτε μετ’ ἀνδράσιν ἢ καὶ ἀρείους.
sentences.l:
“Ajaxes, now to you two to defend yourselves dear let it be,
just such as before you were among men, or even better.
sentences.i: “Ajaxes, now let it be dear to the two of you to defend yourselves, just such men as you were before among men, or even better.
sentences.n: σφῶϊν is the dual dative ‘to you two’, and φίλον ἔστω is ‘let it be dear’, ἔστω being the third singular imperative of εἰμί. ἀμύνεσθαι is the middle infinitive of ἀμύνω ‘ward off’, in the middle ‘defend oneself’, so it takes no object; the same wish is said again at 562 with ἀλέξασθαι. οἷοί περ πάρος ἦτε is ‘just such as you were before’, ἦτε being the plural ‘you were’. ἢ καὶ ἀρείους ‘or even better’ has ἀρείους, the plural of ἀρείων ‘better, braver’, a predicate that goes with an understood ἦτε.

sentences.t:
κεῖται ἀνὴρ ὃς πρῶτος ἐσήλατο τεῖχος Ἀχαιῶν
Σαρπηδών·
sentences.l:
Lies a man who first leapt in at the wall of the Achaeans,
Sarpedon;
sentences.i: There lies the man who was the first to leap in at the wall of the Achaeans, Sarpedon;
sentences.n: κεῖται ‘lies’ is said of the dead man, as at 541. ἐσήλατο is the aorist of ἐσάλλομαι ‘leap in at’, which takes the accusative of the place, τεῖχος, and ὃς πρῶτος is ‘who first’. The wall is the one that the Achaeans built (Book 7, fought over in Book 12); that he was the first is Patroclus’ claim as the speaker, and the name Σαρπηδών is held to the end for emphasis.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἴ μιν ἀεικισσαίμεθ’ ἑλόντες,
τεύχεά τ’ ὤμοιιν ἀφελοίμεθα, καί τιν’ ἑταίρων
αὐτοῦ ἀμυνομένων δαμασαίμεθα νηλέϊ χαλκῷ.
sentences.l:
but if him we might treat unseemly, having taken him,
and the armour from his shoulders we might take off, and some one of his companions
there defending, we might subdue with pitiless bronze.”
sentences.i: But if only we could seize him and abuse him, strip the armour from his shoulders, and overcome one of his companions as they defend him there, with the pitiless bronze.”
sentences.n: εἰ with the optatives ἀεικισσαίμεθ’, ἀφελοίμεθα and δαμασαίμεθα (first plural aorist, middle) has no main clause, and is read as a wish, ‘if only we might’. ἑλόντες ‘having taken’ is an aorist participle, ἀεικίζω ‘treat unseemly’ is the verb of 545, and ὤμοιιν is the dual genitive of ὦμος ‘from the two shoulders’, with ἀφελοίμεθα from ἀφαιρέομαι ‘take away’. καί τιν’ ἑταίρων ‘and some one of his companions’ has the partitive genitive, and αὐτοῦ can be the adverb ‘there, on the spot’ or the genitive ‘him’ with ἀμυνομένων ‘defending’, with the same sense. νηλέϊ χαλκῷ ‘pitiless bronze’ is the usual phrase. Patroclus wishes for the outrage that Glaucus feared; the speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ ἀλέξασθαι μενέαινον.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they themselves also were eager to defend themselves.
sentences.i: So he spoke; they were already eager to defend themselves.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes Patroclus’ speech, and οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the two Ajaxes. καὶ αὐτοί is ‘themselves also’, they were eager already; ἀλέξασθαι is the aorist infinitive middle of ἀλέξω ‘ward off, defend oneself’, and μενέαινον is an imperfect of μενεαίνω ‘be eager’, as at 491. The same words begin a longer unit at 15.565, whose English this follows.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐπεὶ ἀμφοτέρωθεν ἐκαρτύναντο φάλαγγας
Τρῶες καὶ Λύκιοι καὶ Μυρμιδόνες καὶ Ἀχαιοί,
σύμβαλον ἀμφὶ νέκυι κατατεθνηῶτι μάχεσθαι
δεινὸν ἀΰσαντες·
sentences.l:
And they, when on both sides they had made strong their battle-lines,
Trojans and Lycians and Myrmidons and Achaeans,
clashed to fight around the dead man, him who has died,
having shouted terribly;
sentences.i: And when they had strengthened their battle-lines on both sides, Trojans and Lycians and Myrmidons and Achaeans, they clashed together to fight around the dead man, with a terrible shout;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ takes up all the fighters of both sides, and the four names that follow are the subject, in apposition. ἐκαρτύναντο φάλαγγας ‘made strong their battle-lines’ is the phrase of 11.215 and 12.415, ἐκαρτύναντο being a middle aorist, ‘for themselves’; ἀμφοτέρωθεν is ‘from both sides’. The Myrmidons are named apart from the other Achaeans because Patroclus leads them. σύμβαλον is an unaugmented aorist of συμβάλλω ‘clash’, used without an object, with μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ for the purpose. ἀμφὶ νέκυι κατατεθνηῶτι is the phrase of 526, the dead man being Sarpedon. ἀΰσαντες is an aorist participle of ἀΰω ‘shout’, with δεινόν ‘terribly’ as an adverb.

sentences.t: μέγα δ’ ἔβραχε τεύχεα φωτῶν.
sentences.l: and loudly clanged the armour of the men.
sentences.i: and the armour of the men clanged loudly.
sentences.n: ἔβραχε is the aorist of βράχω, and its sense follows its subject (the clanging of bronze at 4.420; the bellowing of Ares at 5.859), here ‘clanged’. The subject τεύχεα ‘armour’ is neuter plural and takes a singular verb, the usual Greek rule. μέγα ‘loudly’ is an adverb, and φωτῶν is the genitive plural of φώς ‘man’.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς δ’ ἐπὶ νύκτ’ ὀλοὴν τάνυσε κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ,
ὄφρα φίλῳ περὶ παιδὶ μάχης ὀλοὸς πόνος εἴη.
sentences.l:
And Zeus over a night baneful stretched, over the strong battle,
so that around his dear son of the fighting a baneful toil might be.
sentences.i: And Zeus stretched a baneful night over the strong battle, so that around his dear son the baneful toil of fighting might be.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … τάνυσε is split (tmesis), ‘stretched over’, with νύκτ’ ὀλοήν ‘baneful night’ as object and κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ ‘the strong battle’ in the dative. ὀλοός ‘baneful’ is the adjective of the night and again of the toil in 568, so the two are tied together. ὄφρα with the optative εἴη ‘might be’ gives the purpose, φίλῳ περὶ παιδί is ‘around his dear son’, with περί and the dative, and μάχης πόνος is ‘the toil of fighting’. The son is Sarpedon, whose body the armies now fight over. Zeus, who let him die, now causes the fight over his body to go on in darkness.
